design_detail: Longitudinal co-twin control study in the E-Risk Longitudinal Twin Study, a nationally representative birth cohort of same-sex twins born in England and Wales in 1994-1995. IQ was measured at 5 and 12 (before almost anyone had used cannabis) and again at 18; executive functions (CANTAB) only at 18. Cannabis was measured once, at 18: DSM-IV past-year dependence and self-reported past-year frequency. Full-sample regressions with twins nested in pairs (SAS SURVEYREG), and within-pair comparisons: 57 pairs discordant for dependence, and twin differences in frequency across 977 complete pairs, monozygotic and dizygotic pairs analysed together. Version read: the author manuscript deposited in PubMed Central (NIHMS894998), not the version of record.
can_establish: Whether adolescents who report cannabis use or meet criteria for dependence at 18 already had lower IQ at 5 and 12, whether their IQ fell more than their peers' between 12 and 18, and how much of the IQ and executive-function differences seen at 18 remain when twins from the same family who differ in cannabis use are compared.
cannot_establish: Effects of heavy, prolonged or adult use (use was measured once, as past-year use at 18, and 3% used daily or more often); any change in executive functions (measured only at 18) or effects on memory (not tested); the absence of a small or moderate effect (57 discordant pairs and no confidence intervals); or confounding by factors that differ between twins of the same family, such as alcohol, tobacco and other drug use, which do not enter these analyses.

sample.recruitment: Birth-register sample (E-Risk): 1,116 families with same-sex twins (93% of those eligible), drawn from a register of twins born in England and Wales in 1994-1995 and first visited at home at age 5 in 1999-2000 (2,232 children). Teenage mothers were over-selected to replace high-risk families lost to non-response and older mothers of twins conceived by assisted reproduction under-selected, so that the families span British socioeconomic conditions; their neighbourhood distribution is compared with national figures, with urban-prosperity areas under-represented (Methods › Participants, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Analytic sample: all cohort members with IQ data at ages 5, 12 and 18 (n=1,989; 96% of the 2,066 seen at 18). No exclusions by psychiatric history, substance use or medical condition are described (Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: 47.26% male; 43.99% dizygotic pairs (56% monozygotic at intake); mean family SES 2.00 (SD 0.82) on a 1 to 3 scale; IQ standardized to mean 100 (SD 15) in the cohort at each age. Boys had slightly higher IQ at 12 and 18 and more past-year use (45.96% vs 30.03%) and dependence (6.06% vs 2.57%) than girls (Table 1). Ethnicity is not reported.
sample.attrition: Participation was 98% at 7, 96% at 10, 96% at 12 and 93% at 18 (n=2,066). Those seen and not seen at 18 did not differ at age 5 in SES (chi-square 0.86, p = .65), IQ (t = 0.98, p = .33), internalizing problems (t = 0.40, p = .69) or externalizing problems (t = 0.41, p = .68). The 77 people seen at 18 who lacked IQ data at one of the three ages are not compared with the analytic sample (Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: A population-representative cohort of same-sex twins with high retention; whether the results apply to singletons is not discussed. Exposure was mostly light: 63% reported no past-year use, 28% use less than monthly, 3% monthly, 3% weekly, 2% daily and 1% many times a day; dependence affected 84 people. Heavy and prolonged use is therefore barely represented, which the authors name as a limitation (Methods › Measures › Cannabis Use, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Interview at 18 only: DSM-IV criteria for past-year cannabis dependence (the interview instrument is not named in the main text) and self-reported past-year frequency on a six-point scale (never, less than monthly, monthly, weekly, daily, many times a day). No biological verification; the authors name possible under-reporting as a limitation (Methods › Measures › Cannabis Use; Discussion, 5th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Past-year frequency at 18 only (distribution under sample.selection_effects); the within-pair correlation for frequency was r = 0.55. Age at first use, duration, cumulative use, route and product strength were not reported. Only 19 participants had tried cannabis by age 12, the last IQ assessment before exposure (Methods › Measures › Intelligence Quotient (IQ), 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled. No alcohol, tobacco or other drug variable enters any reported model: covariates were sex, plus age-5 IQ in the IQ-change analyses and age-12 IQ in the executive-function analyses (Methods › Statistical Analyses, 1st paragraph). The within-pair comparison removes only influences that twins share.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported. The age-18 IQ and CANTAB testing and the cannabis interview were all part of the age-18 phase of the study; whether participants had used cannabis shortly before testing is not reported or analysed.

comparison.controls: Full sample: adolescents without dependence (n=1,905), or less frequent use (frequency treated as a continuous score). Co-twin analyses: the co-twin without dependence in 57 discordant pairs; for frequency, within-pair differences in outcomes regressed on within-pair differences in frequency in all 977 complete pairs (Methods › Statistical Analyses, 3rd paragraph).
comparison.matching: Co-twins share family environment, age and sex (same-sex pairs only) and all (monozygotic) or about half (dizygotic) of their segregating genes. Monozygotic and dizygotic pairs were analysed together to preserve power; the authors report little evidence that associations differed by zygosity, without showing the results (Methods › Statistical Analyses, 3rd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Unusually, IQ was measured before cannabis initiation (ages 5 and 12) and is used as a covariate. Executive functions have no pre-use baseline. Twin-specific premorbid differences (for example childhood conduct or attention problems, or mental health) are not adjusted for; family SES was measured (Table 1) but does not enter the models.

outcomes.instruments: IQ: age 5, WPPSI-R short form (Vocabulary and Block Design, pro-rated); age 12, WISC-R, and age 18, WAIS-IV, each pro-rated from the same two subtests (Information and Matrix Reasoning) and standardized within the cohort to mean 100, SD 15. Executive functions at 18 only: CANTAB Rapid Visual Processing (A prime; total false alarms), Spatial Working Memory (total errors; strategy) and Spatial Span forward and reversed, each standardized to mean 0, SD 1 (Methods › Measures).
outcomes.validity_norms: Scores are standardized within the cohort rather than against published norms, so IQ change is change in standing relative to peers. Full-scale IQ is pro-rated from two subtests, and the 12-to-18 change score spans two Wechsler editions; reliability of the change scores is not reported. Test descriptions are in Supplemental Table 2 (not read).
outcomes.operationalization: IQ decline: age-18 minus age-12 pro-rated IQ (change score), with and without adjustment for age-5 IQ; the authors focus on 12 to 18 because both scores use the same two subtests. Executive-function impairment: a lower standardized score at 18 than the comparison group, with and without adjustment for age-12 IQ. All models adjusted for sex.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Ten outcome measures (IQ at 5, 12 and 18, IQ change, six CANTAB scores), each analysed for two exposures, in the full sample and within pairs, with and without baseline adjustment. The authors say the single significant within-pair result might be a false positive (Discussion, 5th paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Dependence and IQ (Table 2; sex-adjusted means): full sample, dependent vs not, age 5: 95.18 vs 100.41 (difference -5.23, t = -2.94, p = .003); age 12: 94.95 vs 100.56 (-5.61, t = -3.11, p = .002); age 18: 93.14 vs 100.48 (-7.34, t = -5.27, p < .001); change 12 to 18: -1.81 vs -0.08 (difference -1.73, t = -1.27, p = .20; after age-5 IQ -2.02, t = -1.49, p = .14). Discordant pairs (57): age 5: 94.26 vs 93.50 (+0.76, p = .70); age 12: 93.97 vs 95.47 (-1.50, p = .43); age 18: 92.86 vs 94.31 (-1.45, t = -0.81, p = .42); change 0.05 (t = 0.02, p = .98). Frequency and IQ (Table 3; standardized betas): full sample age 5 -0.05 (p = .07), age 12 -0.11, age 18 -0.15 (both p < .001), change -0.05 (p = .035; -0.05, p = .023 after age-5 IQ); within pairs 0.02, 0.03, 0.00 and change -0.02 (p = .46). Dependence and executive functions (Table 4; z-scores): full sample worse on RVP A prime (-0.22 vs 0.02, p = .024), SWM strategy (0.21 vs -0.01, p = .017), Spatial Span Forward (-0.48 vs 0.02, p < .001) and Reversed (-0.33 vs 0.01, p < .001); after age-12 IQ only Spatial Span Forward (-0.35 vs 0.01, p < .001) and Reversed (-0.20 vs 0.01, p = .030); no difference within discordant pairs (all p >= .20). Frequency and executive functions (Table 5): full sample worse on 5 of 6 tests after age-12 IQ (betas -0.05 to -0.09, or 0.06 where higher is worse); within pairs only Spatial Span Reversed, beta -0.07 (p = .036; .022 after age-12 IQ). No confidence intervals are printed. Editors' approximations (SE = estimate / t, or from the two-sided p; normal approximation, t with 56 df for discordant pairs): full-sample dependence and IQ change -1.73, 95% CI about -4.4 to +0.9 points; discordant-pair age-18 IQ difference -1.45, about -5.0 to +2.1; within-pair frequency and IQ change beta -0.02, about -0.07 to +0.03 SD (full sample -0.05, about -0.10 to -0.004); Spatial Span Forward, discordant pairs -0.20 SD, about -0.51 to +0.11, against -0.50 (about -0.71 to -0.29) in the full sample.
analysis.covariates: Sex in all models; age-5 IQ (IQ change) or age-12 IQ (executive functions) in the adjusted models; non-independence of twins handled by Taylor linearization (SAS SURVEYREG). No adjustment for SES, other substance use or psychiatric problems (Methods › Statistical Analyses).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No pre-registration or analysis plan is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All ages, change scores and six executive-function scores are tabulated for both exposures, both samples and both levels of adjustment. The sensitivity analyses (excluding the 19 people who had used cannabis by 12; Information and Matrix Reasoning separately; at least weekly use versus none) are in Supplemental Tables 3 to 7 and are summarized in one sentence each; zygosity-specific results are not shown; no confidence intervals are reported.
analysis.power: No power calculation. The authors note the discordant-twin analyses may have been underpowered and that many estimates were close to zero (Discussion, 5th paragraph). See the editors' approximate intervals under effect_sizes: the data exclude large IQ declines between 12 and 18 more firmly than they exclude executive-function differences.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 1,989 twins followed from 5 to 18, those with past-year cannabis dependence at 18 (n=84) had lower IQ than the rest at 5 (by 5.23 points), at 12 (5.61) and at 18 (7.34), but their IQ did not fall significantly more between 12 and 18 (difference -1.73 points, p = .20; editors' approximate 95% CI -4.4 to +0.9). Within 57 pairs discordant for dependence the twins with dependence did not differ from their co-twins at any age (differences between +0.76 and -1.50 points) or in change (0.05), and both twins in these pairs scored below the cohort mean. More frequent past-year use went with slightly greater IQ decline in the full sample (beta -0.05 SD per SD of frequency, p = .035) but not within pairs (beta -0.02, p = .46). Executive-function scores at 18 were lower with dependence on 4 of 6 CANTAB measures (2 of 6 after age-12 IQ) and with more frequent use on 5 of 6, but not within pairs, except Spatial Span Reversed for frequency (beta -0.07, p = .036; .022 after age-12 IQ).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that short-term adolescent use "does not appear to cause IQ decline or impair executive functions", even at the level of dependence, and that family background factors explain the poorer test performance (Abstract › Conclusions; Discussion, 1st and 6th paragraphs). Gaps: (1) duration of use was never measured: use was assessed once, as past-year use at 18, so short-term is the authors' inference; (2) the within-pair nulls come from 57 discordant pairs and are printed without confidence intervals; the editors' approximations include IQ differences of a few points and executive-function differences up to about half a standard deviation (Spatial Span Forward -0.20 SD within pairs against -0.50 SD in the full sample), so the data rule out large short-term IQ declines more firmly than effects on executive functions; (3) executive functions were measured only at 18, so the study shows that cross-sectional differences shrink within families, not whether these functions changed after use; (4) family background combines shared environment with only part of genetic influence, because monozygotic and dizygotic pairs were pooled, and factors that differ between twins (alcohol, tobacco, other drugs) were not measured; (5) the abstract reports little evidence of IQ decline, although the full-sample frequency analysis found a small significant one, which the Results and Discussion do report. Against this, the Discussion states the limits plainly (self-report, no memory tests, possible lack of power, rare intensive use) and presents the result as compatible with harm that appears only after years of heavy use.

timeline.event: Fried et al. (2002, 2005; refs 12 and 11), a cohort compared with its own pre-drug test performance; the 2005 report is one of the three studies with the greatest exposure that, the authors say, showed the strongest evidence of decline.

Meier et al. (ref. 8), Dunedin: described here as an 8-point IQ decline with dependence that persisted through adulthood and no decline with dependence only at 18; the authors say their null result does not conflict with it.
Rogeberg (2013), critique of the Dunedin analysis (socioeconomic confounding), and the reply by Moffitt et al. (2013): both in the project's Tier A list; neither is cited by this paper.
Hall (ref. 3), cited with other reviews for the consensus that heavy use is associated with neuropsychological impairment.
Broyd et al. (ref. 5), cited for the consensus and for previously inconsistent findings on working memory, the authors' reason to doubt their one within-pair result.
Curran et al. (ref. 6), cited for the consensus that heavy use is associated with neuropsychological impairment.
Auer et al. (ref. 9), CARDIA: with Dunedin, the longest follow-up and greatest exposure, and the strongest evidence of decline, as characterized here.

Jackson et al. (ref. 14), two US longitudinal twin studies with a co-twin design, and Mokrysz et al. (ref. 15, ALSPAC) and Castellanos-Ryan et al. (ref. 16): adolescent cohorts described as finding no IQ decline; Jackson et al. and Castellanos-Ryan et al. are the two cohorts said to find some evidence that lower IQ or executive functions preceded use.
Boccio and Beaver (ref. 17), on adolescent use and adult intelligence, grouped with the adolescent cohorts described as finding no IQ decline; the paper gives no further detail.
This study, published online 5 September 2017 (issue February 2018).

Scott et al., meta-analysis of cognition in adolescents and young adults (read in this round): cites this study, with Jackson et al. (2016), as large-scale evidence questioning cannabis as a cause of cognitive change once confounding and familial factors are taken into account.
Later tests in the project's lists, not cited here: co-twin control analyses by Schaefer et al. (2021, 2022) and the Dunedin follow-up at 45 (Meier et al., 2022).

replication.where_it_stands: One of the few designs that combine IQ measured before use with a within-family comparison. Its null result for adolescent IQ decline agrees with the other adolescent cohorts it cites (Jackson et al., 2016; Mokrysz et al., 2016; Castellanos-Ryan et al., 2016; Boccio and Beaver, 2017, as described here), whereas cohorts with longer and heavier exposure (Dunedin; CARDIA) reported decline; whether lower IQ precedes use is mixed across cohorts (by the authors' count, four of six found no earlier difference, two some). Claims should cite it for the absence of a detectable IQ decline between 12 and 18 at the mostly light exposure levels of a British birth cohort, and for familial confounding of IQ differences at 18, with the approximate intervals; not for the absence of effects of sustained heavy use, of effects on memory, or of effects on executive functions.

funding.funder: The E-Risk Study is funded by the UK Medical Research Council (grant G1002190), with additional support from NICHD grant HD077482 and the Jacobs Foundation; H. L. Fisher is supported by an MQ: Transforming Mental Health Fellowship (MQ14F40) (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the PMC author manuscript contains no declaration-of-interests statement; the version of record, which may carry one, was not read.
funding.affiliations_note: Arizona State University; Duke University (psychology and neuroscience; psychiatry); King's College London (MRC Social, Genetic and Developmental Psychiatry Centre; child and adolescent psychiatry); a London foundation trust. Meier, Caspi and Houts are among the listed authors of the Dunedin IQ report (ref. 8) that the Discussion reconciles with this null result. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A large population cohort that tests cognition, including memory, before any cannabis use and repeatedly afterwards, records frequency, product strength and duration at every wave, follows people with sustained heavy use into adulthood, and compares twins or siblings who differ in use while adjusting for alcohol, tobacco and other between-twin differences, reporting within-family estimates with confidence intervals; the authors point to the ABCD study (about 10,000 children followed from age 9-10) as the kind of cohort needed.

domains.note: Judged for the within-pair estimates that carry the conclusions: they remove shared family environment and part of genetic influence (fully only in monozygotic pairs, which were pooled with dizygotic pairs), but nothing that differs between twins, such as alcohol, tobacco, other drug use or childhood behaviour problems, is measured or adjusted. The full-sample estimates, adjusted only for sex and baseline IQ, are at high risk of confounding, which is the paper's own point.

One self-report of past-year frequency and a DSM-IV past-year dependence assessment, both at 18, with no biological check, age at onset, duration, cumulative use or potency. The 12-to-18 IQ change is set against use measured only at its end. Misclassification is probably unrelated to IQ change and so biases toward no association, more strongly for within-pair differences (twin correlation for frequency 0.55), which matters for a null result.
Population-representative birth cohort; 93% seen at 18 with no age-5 differences between those seen and not seen; 96% of those seen are analysed.
None relevant reported; treatment for cannabis problems is not mentioned.
1,989 of 2,232 children (89%) analysed; a few CANTAB scores missing (Ns 1,895 to 1,902 non-dependent, 83 to 84 dependent). The 77 seen at 18 without complete IQ data are not compared.

Standard tests, but IQ at 12 and 18 is pro-rated from two subtests of different Wechsler editions and standardized within the cohort; executive functions were measured only at 18; blinding of testers to cannabis use and recent use or intoxication at testing are not reported.

No pre-registration, but every IQ age, the change score and all six CANTAB scores are reported for both exposures, both samples and both adjustment levels; sensitivity analyses are summarized from the supplement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The co-twin design with IQ measured before use is one of the stronger observational tests of whether adolescent cannabis use lowers IQ, and selection, attrition and reporting are well handled. The concerns are twin-specific confounding (no alcohol, tobacco or other drug measures), an exposure measured once at 18, and outcomes standardized within the cohort, with executive functions measured only once. Beyond bias, imprecision limits what the null can show: the within-pair estimates rest on 57 discordant pairs, no intervals are printed, and heavy use was rare. Cite it for: lower childhood IQ predating dependence; no detectable IQ decline from 12 to 18 with dependence or frequency, in the full sample or within pairs; familial confounding of IQ differences at 18. Do not cite it for: the absence of effects of sustained heavy use, effects on memory, or a change in executive functions.

key_findings.finding: E-Risk cohort: 2,232 children from 1,116 families with same-sex twins (93% of those eligible) assessed at 5 in 1999-2000; participation 98% at 7, 96% at 10 and 12, 93% at 18 (n=2,066). Those seen and not seen at 18 did not differ at age 5 in SES, IQ, internalizing or externalizing problems (all p >= .33). 1,989 participants (96% of those seen at 18) had IQ at 5, 12 and 18: 47.26% male, 43.99% dizygotic.

Exposure at 18: 84 participants (4%; 4.22% in Table 1) met DSM-IV criteria for past-year cannabis dependence; of 977 complete pairs, 908 were concordant for no dependence, 12 concordant for dependence and 57 discordant. Past-year frequency: never 63%, less than monthly 28%, monthly 3%, weekly 3%, daily 2%, many times a day 1%; twin correlation for frequency r = 0.55. 37.56% had used in the past year (girls 30.03%, boys 45.96%). Only 19 participants had tried cannabis by age 12.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Measures › Cannabis Use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Measures › Intelligence Quotient (IQ), 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: Exposure is past-year use at 18 only; no measure of age at onset, duration, cumulative use or potency.

key_findings.finding: Full sample, dependence (n=84) vs no dependence (n=1,905), sex-adjusted mean IQ: age 5, 95.18 vs 100.41 (difference -5.23, t = -2.94, p = .003); age 12, 94.95 vs 100.56 (-5.61, t = -3.11, p = .002); age 18, 93.14 vs 100.48 (-7.34, t = -5.27, p < .001). Change from 12 to 18: -1.81 vs -0.08 points (difference -1.73, t = -1.27, p = .20). After adjustment for age-5 IQ: age 12, -2.80 (p = .08); age 18, -4.82 (t = -3.88, p < .001); change, -2.02 (t = -1.49, p = .14).
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between Cannabis Dependence and IQ, 1st paragraph; Table 2, full-sample rows
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (SE = difference / t, normal approximation): 95% CI for the difference in change about -4.4 to +0.9 IQ points (-4.7 to +0.6 after age-5 IQ). IQ is standardized within the cohort at each age, so change means change relative to peers.

key_findings.finding: 57 pairs discordant for dependence, sex-adjusted mean IQ of the twin with dependence vs the co-twin without: age 5, 94.26 vs 93.50 (+0.76, t = 0.39, p = .70); age 12, 93.97 vs 95.47 (-1.50, t = -0.80, p = .43); age 18, 92.86 vs 94.31 (-1.45, t = -0.81, p = .42); change 12 to 18, -1.11 vs -1.16 (0.05, t = 0.02, p = .98); similar after age-5 IQ. Both twins in discordant pairs scored below the cohort mean, which the authors read as family factors confounding the full-sample association.
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between Cannabis Dependence and IQ, 2nd paragraph; Table 2, Discordant Twins rows
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (t with 56 df): age-18 difference -1.45, 95% CI about -5.0 to +2.1 points; the interval for the change score cannot be computed reliably from the printed t of 0.02.

key_findings.finding: Results for the full sample and the discordant pairs were similar after excluding the 19 participants who had used cannabis by age 12, and for the Information and Matrix Reasoning subtests separately.
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between Cannabis Dependence and IQ, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Values are in Supplemental Tables 3 to 5, not read.

key_findings.finding: Frequency of past-year use at 18 (standardized betas, sex-adjusted): full sample (n=1,989) age-5 IQ -0.05 (p = .07), age-12 IQ -0.11 (p < .001), age-18 IQ -0.15 (p < .001), IQ change 12 to 18 -0.05 (p = .035; -0.05, p = .023 after age-5 IQ), described as an additional decline of 0.05 SD per SD of frequency. Within pairs (977 pairs): 0.02 (p = .56), 0.03 (p = .32), 0.00 (p = .94) and change -0.02 (p = .46; .47 after age-5 IQ). At least weekly use versus none: little evidence of greater IQ decline.
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between Frequency of Cannabis Use and IQ, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (SE from the two-sided p, normal approximation; betas rounded to two decimals): within-pair change beta about -0.07 to +0.03 SD; full sample about -0.10 to -0.004. The weekly-use comparison is in Supplemental Table 6, not read.

key_findings.finding: Dependence and executive functions at 18 (sex-adjusted z-scores, dependent vs not): full sample worse on RVP A prime (-0.22 vs 0.02, t = -2.26, p = .024), SWM strategy (0.21 vs -0.01, t = 2.40, p = .017; higher is worse), Spatial Span Forward (-0.48 vs 0.02, t = -4.57, p < .001) and Spatial Span Reversed (-0.33 vs 0.01, t = -3.37, p < .001); not on RVP false alarms (p = .83) or SWM errors (p = .07). After age-12 IQ, only Spatial Span Forward (-0.35 vs 0.01, t = -3.60, p < .001) and Reversed (-0.20 vs 0.01, t = -2.17, p = .030). Discordant pairs: no significant differences on any test (p = .20 to .72); for example Spatial Span Forward -0.38 vs -0.18 (t = -1.30, p = .20).
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between Cannabis Dependence and Executive Functions, 1st paragraph; Table 4
key_findings.note: Executive functions were measured only at 18 (no pre-use baseline). Editors' calculation (t with 56 df): the discordant-pair Spatial Span Forward difference of -0.20 SD has a 95% CI of about -0.51 to +0.11, compatible with the full-sample difference of -0.50 (about -0.71 to -0.29).

key_findings.finding: Frequency and executive functions at 18 (standardized betas): in the full sample (n=1,978 to 1,985) more frequent use went with worse performance on every test except RVP false alarms, also after age-12 IQ (for example Spatial Span Forward -0.13, then -0.09; both p < .001). Within pairs (967 to 974 pairs) the associations were not significant except Spatial Span Reversed, beta -0.07 (p = .036; -0.07, p = .022 after age-12 IQ), which the authors call small and possibly a false positive. At least weekly use versus none gave similar findings.
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between Frequency of Cannabis Use and Executive Functions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 5; Discussion, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: The weekly-use comparison is in Supplemental Table 7, not read.

key_findings.finding: The authors place their result beside earlier cohorts: of six cohorts with tests before first use, four found no evidence that lower IQ preceded use and two found some; across nine cohorts with repeated testing, those with the longest follow-up (Dunedin; CARDIA) and greatest exposure showed the strongest evidence of decline, and adolescent cohorts with light use the weakest.
key_findings.locator: Introduction (unheaded, after the Abstract), 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand: the per-study details are in Supplemental Table 1, not read.

key_findings.finding: The Discussion describes its own group's Dunedin report as showing an 8-point IQ decline in people with dependence persisting through adulthood and no decline in people dependent only at 18, and calls the adolescent null results consistent with it and with four recent cohorts, one using a co-twin design.
key_findings.note: Second-hand figure from Meier et al. (2012); claim writers should take Dunedin numbers from that paper (see reporting issue 4: the Discussion's time frame and its single-wave statement are inaccurate).

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: self-reported use without biological tests; no tests of memory; discordant-twin analyses possibly underpowered, although many estimates were close to zero; intensive use (many times a day) at 1% prevalence was too rare to test, and very large cohorts such as ABCD (about 10,000 children followed from 9-10 for 10 years) are needed.

Conclusions: short-term adolescent use does not appear to cause IQ decline or impair executive functions, even at the level of dependence; family background explains the poorer test performance of adolescents who use cannabis; neuropsychological functions should be tested before initiation; impairment may develop only with long-term persistent use, which needs further research.
Funding: UK Medical Research Council (G1002190), NICHD (HD077482), the Jacobs Foundation and an MQ fellowship (MQ14F40). No declaration of interests in the author manuscript.

reporting_issues.issue: The within-pair association of frequency with Spatial Span Reversed is given as beta -0.07, p = .036 in the abstract and as p = .022 in the Results text; Table 5 shows these are the estimates before and after adjustment for age-12 IQ, and neither place says which model it reports.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Findings; Results › Associations between Frequency of Cannabis Use and Executive Functions, 1st paragraph; Table 5
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; a claim should name the model (p = .036 sex-adjusted, p = .022 also adjusted for age-12 IQ).

reporting_issues.issue: No confidence interval is printed for any estimate, and the within-pair results (57 discordant pairs) are summarized as showing no differences.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers cannot see what size of effect the null results exclude; the editors' approximations under analysis.effect_sizes show intervals compatible with IQ differences of a few points and executive-function differences of up to about half a standard deviation within pairs.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives 63% for no past-year use at 18, while Table 1 gives 37.56% with past-year use in the analytic sample, which implies 62.44% (editors' arithmetic); the frequency percentages may refer to all 2,066 seen at 18.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Measures › Cannabis Use, 2nd paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; quote Table 1 for the analytic sample.

reporting_issues.issue: Within-pair estimates pool monozygotic and dizygotic pairs; the statement that associations differed little by zygosity is not supported by any reported estimate.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Statistical Analyses, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The share of the familial confounding that is genetic cannot be judged; family background in the conclusions means shared environment plus part of genetic influence.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion describes the Dunedin result as an 8-point IQ decline 'from age 18–38' in people whose dependence persisted through adulthood, and says that people dependent only at 18 did not show IQ decline. Meier et al. (2012) measured change from childhood IQ (mean of ages 7 to 13) to 38 and had no IQ test at 18; in its Fig. 2 the matching group (dependence before 18 at one wave, 17 people) changed by about −0.22 SD (about 3 points), not significantly different from adult onset (p = .44), with no test against no change; and the 8 points refer to the 23 people with adolescent-onset dependence at 3 or more waves, read from a figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Discussion misstates the time frame and the single-wave result of the 2012 Dunedin paper; Dunedin figures should be taken from Meier et al. (2012) itself (this round's Broyd et al. and Curran et al. cards record that reviews give the decline as about 6 or about 8 points).

reporting_issues.issue: The PMC author manuscript has no declaration-of-interests statement.
reporting_issues.consequence: Conflicts cannot be recorded from the version read; the version of record should be checked when the reference record is built.

(2016) and Curran et al. (2016) record that reviews give the Dunedin decline differently (about 6 or about 8 points), so the figure should be taken from Meier et al. (2012) itself.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 214, corrected: not merely ambiguous but wrong on two points: Dunedin measured change from childhood (7-13) to 38, with no IQ test at 18; and the single-wave adolescent-onset group (n = 17) changed by about -0.22 SD, not significantly different from adult onset (p = .44), with no test against no change.
